title: Never Heard Of Lucy Calkins? Here’s Why You Should Have
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Natalie Wexler argues that the controversy over Lucy Calkins' Units of Study matters well beyond reading teachers because balanced literacy conflicts with cognitive science on both word recognition and comprehension. She notes that Calkins and Fountas and Pinnell together reach an estimated 60% of reading teachers, and that Calkins plans to change her phonics approach after harsh ratings from EdReports and Student Achievement Partners. Her own claim goes further: unless the comprehension approach also changes, many students will not become fully literate. That approach foregrounds skills and strategies over content, practised on easy texts at each child's level, whereas cognitive science shows that you need knowledge and academic vocabulary to learn from complex text. Wexler supports this with classroom observations of a second-grade lesson on finding the topic of a chapter on ponies and a fifth-grade lesson on author's perspective that she found hollow. She concludes that building knowledge through read-alouds and discussion, alongside systematic phonics on a separate track, is the better path, especially for children from less educated families.
points: Balanced literacy curricula, including Calkins' and Fountas and Pinnell's, reach an estimated 60% of reading teachers, so the dispute has real stakes for achievement.
Wexler says phonics reform is not enough, because skills-and-strategies comprehension instruction still leaves knowledge unbuilt.
Cognitive science holds that readers need topic knowledge and academic vocabulary to gain knowledge from complex text, which coherent topic sequences can provide.
Her classroom visits show strategy lessons, such as finding the topic of Ponies, that are detached from interesting content and do not build vocabulary.
Text complexity and knowledge building are linked, and teacher read-alouds with content discussion are the most effective route until about age 13.
quotes: If you’re not a reading teacher, you may not know who Lucy Calkins is, and the controversy over her curriculum may seem like inside baseball. But understanding it is crucial to improving reading outcomes and general academic achievement, especially for children from less educated families.
What’s put in the foreground is a series of strategies rather than any particular content. The topic may be clouds one day and zebras the next.

The problem, as cognitive scientists have long understood, is that you need to first have some knowledge—either of the topic or of general academic vocabulary—in order to gain knowledge from written text, especially as it gets more complex.

She turned to a chapter called “Wild Ponies” and read aloud the title and then raced through the text, emphasizing the words “wild ponies” while mumbling other words the kids were unlikely to be familiar with, like Chincoteague.

Both organizations treat “text complexity” as a separate criterion from “building knowledge,” when in fact the two go hand-in-hand. The only way to equip students to read complex text is to build their academic knowledge.

It’s been found that children can take in more complex concepts and vocabulary through listening than through their own reading until about age 13, on average. Once they’ve acquired knowledge about a topic through listening and discussion, it can fuel their ability to read and write about that topic.

Let’s not underestimate kids. If they see and hear an adult reading a book to them, and are then guided to discuss and think about its content, they should get the idea that reading is about more than decoding.
